name: Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls
question: Which calls can go out together?
summary: A model can emit several independent calls in one turn. Your code can run them concurrently, so the wait becomes the slowest call instead of the sum. A call that needs another call’s output must wait for it. All results go back together, and a failure in the batch must not drop its siblings.
useCases: Several independent lookups per request: KYC checks, fare searches
Fan-out reads across services before one decision
Latency-sensitive assistants where every second counts

items.detail: wall-clock falls from the sum to the critical path
all tool_result blocks in one user message, before any text
each failed or skipped call still gets a result with is_error
a call that needs another’s output runs after it
BFCL scores simple, multiple, parallel and parallel-multiple calls

steps: Collect every tool_use block in the response
Classify each call: independent read, dependent, or side-effecting
Run independent calls together with per-call timeouts; run dependent calls in order
Return one message with all results, errors marked, then measure the critical path
pitfalls: Running a dependent call in the same batch as its input: it reads an id that does not exist yet
Letting one exception cancel the batch so no results go back
Splitting results across messages, which discourages parallel calls later
remember: Sum becomes max, but only for calls that do not depend on each other.
caption: Illustrative KYC latencies. The four lookups run together; open_account waits for all four.

code.text: except Exception as e:                        # never drop a result
calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
reads = [c for c in calls if c.name in READS]
rest = [c for c in calls if c.name not in READS]  # writes, dependents
results = list(await asyncio.gather(*(run_one(c) for c in reads)))
failed = any(r.get("is_error") for r in results)
for c in rest:                                # in order, after the join
return {"role": "user", "content": results}   # all results, one message

steps.title: Collect every call
steps.text: One response can contain several tool_use blocks. Here the model asks for four KYC lookups at once: PAN, CKYC, Aadhaar OTP status and the credit bureau.

steps.title: Classify each call
steps.text: The four lookups only read and do not need each other’s output, so they can run together. Writes and calls that need another call’s result go to a second group.

steps.title: Run the reads together
steps.text: asyncio.gather starts all four at once, each with its own timeout. The wait becomes the slowest lookup, 1,200 ms, not the 3,400 ms sum.

steps.title: Run dependent calls after the join
steps.text: open_account needs all four results, so it runs only after the join: 1,200 + 400 = 1,600 ms. In practice it often arrives in the model’s next turn.

steps.title: Return every result in one message
steps.text: A failed call returns is_error true, and a call skipped because of it says so. All results go back in one user message, one per tool_use_id.

steps.title: Measure the critical path
steps.text: Wall-clock time is the longest chain of dependent calls: bureau (1,200 ms), then open_account (400 ms). Adding more independent lookups barely changes it.

pros: Wall-clock time falls from the sum of calls to the critical path
No extra model turns: several calls come back in one message
Simple to add with asyncio or a thread pool
Scales well for fan-out reads across services
cons: Hidden dependencies cause races and wrong results
More concurrent requests can hit rate limits
Failure handling is harder: one call can fail while others succeed
Side-effecting calls need a defined order
avoidWhen: Every call needs the previous one’s output
Writes whose order matters, such as debit then credit

playgroundGuide.scenario: A stockbroker’s onboarding agent opens a demat account. In one turn it asks for five calls: PAN verification (600 ms), CKYC search (700 ms), Aadhaar OTP status (900 ms), a credit bureau pull (1,200 ms) and open_account (400 ms), which needs all four checks. Each card lets you change a call’s latency and what it depends on.
controls: Set each call’s latency and, from the second call on, which earlier call it depends on.
Run independent calls in sequence or in parallel.
Make bureau_pull time out, and choose whether errors are caught per call.

outputs.name: Timeline

outputs.name: Wall-clock time
outputs.meaning: When the last call finishes, against the sum of all latencies.

outputs.name: Critical path
outputs.meaning: Number of calls in the longest dependent chain.

outputs.name: Results returned
outputs.meaning: tool_result blocks sent back; every tool_use id needs one.

outputs.name: Verdict
outputs.meaning: Time saved, or why the request fails.

presets.name: One after another
presets.expect: Every call waits for the previous one: 3,800 ms wall-clock, a critical path of all 5 calls.

presets.name: Fan out, then open
presets.expect: The four lookups run together; open_account waits for the bureau: 1,600 ms, 2.38× faster, critical path 2 calls.

presets.name: A timeout, uncaught
presets.expect: bureau_pull times out and the exception aborts the batch: 0 of 5 results are returned and the request fails.

presets.name: A hidden chain
presets.expect: CKYC waits for PAN and Aadhaar waits for CKYC: 2,600 ms, with a critical path of 4 calls.

missions.text: Bring wall-clock time under 1,000 ms with all 5 results returned.
missions.hint: Parallel first. Then shorten the slowest input of open_account, or ask whether open_account really needs every lookup.

missions.text: With bureau_pull timing out, still return all 5 results.
missions.hint: Catch errors per call: the timeout returns is_error, and open_account returns “Not executed”.

missions.text: In parallel, make the critical path exactly 3 calls long.
missions.hint: Make one lookup depend on another so that chain finishes after the bureau call.

tools.ex: The model asks for four KYC lookups at once; the app returns four tool_result blocks together.
pros: A setting inside tool_choice turns it off when order matters
cons: Your executor must run the calls concurrently
Splitting results across messages discourages later parallel calls

goals: Identify which calls in a turn are independent
Calculate wall-clock time from latencies and dependencies
Return complete, correctly marked results when one call fails

practice.scenario: A travel agent is asked for the cheapest Delhi–Bengaluru trip next Friday. In one turn the model asks for three airline fare searches and a hotel availability check; the app runs all four at once, so the wait is the slowest search rather than the sum. Booking the chosen flight and hotel happens afterwards, in sequence, because each booking needs a fare id from the searches.

industries.use: PAN, CKYC, Aadhaar-OTP status and bureau checks run together before account opening
Fare and hotel searches fan out; bookings run one at a time
Stock, price and delivery-estimate lookups for a basket in one turn

practice.analogy: Ordering at a food court. You place orders at three counters at once and wait only for the slowest one, but you can’t pay for the meal until every counter has told you the price.

library.name: Python asyncio + Anthropic SDK
library.what: asyncio.gather runs the independent calls concurrently; each gets its own timeout and its own tool_result.

practice.note: TOOLS maps tool names to your async functions. Results are returned in the order the model asked for them.

samples.code:
import asyncio, json

READS = {"search_fares", "hotel_availability"}          # independent, no side effects

async def run_one(block, timeout=5.0):
    try:
        out = await asyncio.wait_for(TOOLS[block.name](**block.input), timeout)
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": json.dumps(out)}
    except Exception as e:                               # a failure never drops its siblings
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": f"Error: {e!r}", "is_error": True}

async def run_turn(resp):
    calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    reads = [c for c in calls if c.name in READS]
    others = [c for c in calls if c.name not in READS]
    results = list(await asyncio.gather(*(run_one(c) for c in reads)))
    for c in others:                                     # dependent or side-effecting: in order
        results.append(await run_one(c))
    order = {c.id: i for i, c in enumerate(calls)}
    results.sort(key=lambda r: order[r["tool_use_id"]])
    return {"role": "user", "content": results}          # all results in one message

numericDrill.question: Calls A (300 ms), B (800 ms) and C (500 ms) are independent. D (400 ms) needs B’s output. E (200 ms) needs both C and D. With unlimited concurrency, what is the wall-clock time in ms?
numericDrill.answer: A, B and C start at 0. D starts when B ends at 800 and ends at 1,200. E waits for C (500) and D (1,200), so it runs 1,200–1,400. Wall-clock 1,400 ms against 2,200 ms in sequence. The critical path is B → D → E.

interview.question: How do you decide which tool calls in one turn can run in parallel?
interview.answer: Calls that only read and do not need each other’s output can run together. A call whose arguments come from another call’s result must wait, and side-effecting calls usually run one at a time in a defined order. The speed-up is bounded by the critical path, the longest chain of dependent calls.

interview.question: One call in a parallel batch fails. What do you send back?
interview.answer: A result for every call. The failed one gets is_error: true with a clear message; calls skipped because of it get an error such as “Not executed: the preceding call failed”. All results go in one user message. Dropping results leaves call ids unanswered and the request is rejected.

mistakes.mistake: Putting a call and the call that needs its output in one gather
mistakes.fix: Run dependent calls after the call they depend on

mistakes.mistake: Letting one exception cancel the whole batch
mistakes.fix: Catch per call and return every result, errors marked

quiz.question: A KYC turn asks for PAN (600 ms), CKYC (700 ms), Aadhaar OTP status (900 ms) and bureau (1,200 ms) checks, all independent. Run concurrently, how long do they take?
quiz.explanation: Concurrent independent calls finish with the slowest one: 1,200 ms.

quiz.question: In the same flow, open_account (400 ms) needs all four checks. What is the wall-clock time for the whole turn?
quiz.explanation: 1,200 ms for the slowest check, then 400 ms: 1,600 ms.

quiz.question: Calls A (300 ms), B (800 ms) and C (500 ms) are independent. D (400 ms) needs B. E (200 ms) needs C and D. What is the wall-clock time?
How should results from three parallel tool calls be returned to Claude?
options: All three tool_result blocks in one user message, before any text
As plain text in the next user question
quiz.explanation: All results go in one user message; splitting them discourages later parallel calls.

quiz.question: A batch runs create_order and charge_card(order_id=...) together in one gather. What is wrong?
options: The charge depends on the order id, so it must run after create_order succeeds
quiz.explanation: A call that needs another call’s output, especially a write, must wait for it.

quiz.question: A plan-comparison turn fans out four price lookups; one times out. What should the response to the model contain? Select all that apply.
options: One result with is_error for the timeout
All four tool_result blocks in one message
No results, because the batch failed
quiz.explanation: Every call gets a result; the failure is marked, not allowed to drop its siblings.

quiz.question: Which Claude setting turns off parallel tool calls?
With tool_choice auto and disable_parallel_tool_use true, how many tool calls can one response contain?
quiz.explanation: With auto it can make at most one call; with any or tool, exactly one.

quiz.question: Four independent carrier-rate calls take 400, 900, 650 and 1,100 ms. How much time does running them in parallel save over sequential?
quiz.explanation: Sequential 3,050 ms; parallel 1,100 ms; saved 1,950 ms.

quiz.question: Which calls are safe to put in the same parallel batch? Select all that apply.
options: Approve the claim, then pay it out
Create a payout that needs the approval id
quiz.explanation: Independent reads can run together; the approval and the payout that depends on it cannot.

quiz.question: A lab agent makes 6 independent calls of 500 ms each, but a partner API allows only 2 concurrent requests. What is the fastest possible wall-clock time?
quiz.explanation: Three waves of two calls: 3 × 500 = 1,500 ms.

quiz.question: A research agent adds a fifth independent 700 ms lookup to four others whose slowest takes 1,100 ms. What happens to wall-clock time?
quiz.explanation: The new call finishes before the slowest existing one, so the critical path is unchanged.

quiz.question: In asyncio, one call in gather raises and you did not catch it. What is the risk?
options: Nothing; other results are still returned
The exception propagates, and without per-call handling you return no results for the batch
The failed call is retried automatically
quiz.explanation: Catch errors per call so every call still produces a result.

quiz.question: Which benchmark categories does BFCL cover? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: BFCL scores simple, multiple, parallel and parallel-multiple calls, plus multi-turn tasks from v3.

quiz.question: A dependent chain is 300 → 500 → 200 ms, and two other independent calls take 700 and 900 ms. What is the wall-clock time?
quiz.explanation: The chain takes 1,000 ms, longer than 900 ms, so it is the critical path.

quiz.question: A travel agent checks three airlines and a hotel at once, then books. Why must the flight and hotel bookings run after the searches?
options: Each booking needs a fare or room id returned by a search
The model cannot emit two calls
quiz.explanation: Bookings depend on search output and have side effects, so they wait.

quiz.question: Which statements about parallel tool calls are true? Select all that apply.
options: The speed-up is bounded by the longest dependent chain
A skipped call should still return a result
Parallel calls always reduce cost per token
Every call in a batch must use the same tool
quiz.explanation: Critical path bounds the speed-up and every call needs a result. Parallelism does not change token prices, and calls can use different tools.

quiz.question: Five independent calls take 200 ms each. Run sequentially they take 1,000 ms. Run in parallel, what is the speed-up?
A call is skipped because the call it depended on failed. What should its result say?
options: An error such as “Not executed: the preceding call failed”
The result of the failed call
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s guidance returns an is_error result explaining it was not executed.

quiz.question: A dispatcher’s fan-out of 40 lookups triggers 429 errors. Which fixes help? Select all that apply.
options: Increase the number of concurrent calls to finish sooner
quiz.explanation: Limiting concurrency and backing off with jitter respect the rate limit; more concurrency makes it worse.
